children.label: a
children.prompt: A page of writing is reflected in a mirror. Is the image congruent to the real page?

answer.worked: Reflection preserves size and shape, so the mirror image is congruent to the page.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Think of two large jacaranda trees that you have seen. Are they congruent?

answer.worked: The trees have different branching shapes and cannot coincide exactly, even if their overall sizes are similar.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Is a model of the Sydney Harbour Bridge congruent to the real bridge?

answer.worked: The model is smaller than the real bridge. Congruent figures must have the same size as well as the same shape.

children.label: d
children.prompt: Two identical twins stand at attention in army uniform. Are they congruent?

answer.worked: Treating the twins as identical in size and shape and standing in the same pose gives congruent figures. In reality, small physical differences make this approximate.

children.label: e
children.prompt: Think of two cumulus clouds of about the same size. Are they congruent?

answer.worked: Having approximately the same size is insufficient: the clouds have different shapes and do not coincide exactly.

children.label: f
children.prompt: Are two copies of the same photograph congruent?

answer.short: Yes, if printed at the same size.
answer.worked: Copies printed at the same size have matching shapes and dimensions and can be placed exactly on top of one another.

inlines.text: What lower-case letter, apart from b itself, is congruent to b?

answer.short: d or p; possibly q, depending on the font.
answer.worked: A reflection across a vertical line can map b to d, and a reflection across a horizontal line can map b to p. A half-turn may map b to q, depending on the font.

inlines.text: What digit, apart from 9 itself, is congruent to 9?

answer.worked: Rotating 9 through $180^{\circ}$ gives 6 in the usual matching digit style.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise fixed-side rigidity and justify equal rope lengths by applying congruence tests to physical situations.

content.prompt: For class discussion.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Three metal rods, of lengths 2 m, 3 m and 4 m, are bolted together with hinges at the corners. What congruence test explains why the structure is rigid?

answer.worked: The three rods fix all three side lengths of the triangle. By SSS, every triangle with these side lengths is congruent, so its angles cannot change and the structure is rigid.

children.label: b
children.prompt: A rope is attached to the top of a vertical pole. The rope is then tied down to the ground so that it makes an angle of $20^\circ$ to the vertical. Another identical pole nearby is secured in the same way. Assume the ground is horizontal at both poles and the ropes are taut. Do the two ropes necessarily have the same length? Why or why not?

answer.short: Yes. The triangles are congruent by AAS, so the matching rope lengths are equal.
answer.worked: Each pole, rope and ground segment forms a triangle. The angle at each pole’s base is $90^\circ$, the angle between each rope and pole is $20^\circ$, and the matching pole lengths are equal. The triangles are congruent by AAS, so the ropes have equal lengths as matching sides of congruent triangles.

teachingContext.methodNote: Page 8 establishes SSS and that three fixed sides determine the angles. Pages 9–11 explain matching sides, AAS and conclusions from corresponding sides of congruent triangles. Page 13 applies SSS with a common side; its final Example 5 conclusion contains triangle symbols where angle symbols are intended.
teachingContext.mappingNote: Part a applies SSS to rigidity. Part b applies AAS using equal pole lengths, equal 20-degree angles and right angles under the explicitly added horizontal-ground assumption. Neither task requires trigonometry.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Using a ruler and compasses only, construct a triangle with side lengths of 6 cm, 8 cm and 5 cm.

answer.short: A triangle with sides 6 cm, 8 cm and 5 cm, constructed using intersecting compass arcs.
answer.worked: Draw $AB=8$ cm. Draw an arc with centre $A$ and radius 6 cm, then an arc with centre $B$ and radius 5 cm. Label an intersection $C$. Join $AC$ and $BC$, retaining the construction arcs. Either reflected position of $C$ is valid.

spec.description: Authored solution construction with an 8 cm baseline and intersecting arcs of radii 6 cm and 5 cm. No diagram is supplied in the student source.
spec.mathematics: AB=8 cm, AC=6 cm and BC=5 cm; C is an intersection of the two compass arcs.

children.label: i
children.prompt: What happens when you try to construct a triangle with side lengths of 4 cm, 5 cm and 12 cm?

answer.short: It is impossible: $4+5=9<12$, so the compass circles do not intersect.
answer.worked: Draw a 12 cm baseline. Circles centred at its endpoints with radii 4 cm and 5 cm do not meet, because $4+5=9<12$. There is no third vertex, so the triangle cannot be constructed.

inlines.text: Copy and complete: ‘The longest side of a triangle …’
The longest side of a triangle

inlines.answer: is shorter than the sum of the other two sides.

answer.short: The longest side of a triangle is shorter than the sum of the other two sides.
answer.worked: The longest side must be shorter than the sum of the other two sides. This is the triangle inequality; otherwise the two shorter sides cannot meet to form a triangle.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Jack says that in the Great Outback there are three towns $A$, $B$ and $C$. Town $B$ is 34 km from $A$ and 68 km from $C$. Town $A$ is 110 km from $C$. (All distances are as the crow flies.) Comment on Jack’s claim.

answer.short: Jack’s claim is false: $34+68=102<110$, contradicting the triangle inequality.
answer.worked:
$$AB+BC=34+68=102\text{ km}$$
The direct distance $AC$ cannot exceed the distance from $A$ to $C$ via $B$. Since $110>102$, the stated distances are impossible, so Jack’s claim is false.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Using a ruler and compasses only, construct a triangle $ABC$ in which $AB=12\text{ cm}$, $\angle A=45^\circ$ and $\angle B=60^\circ$. Measure the length of $AC$ to the nearest millimetre. Which congruence test tells you that your neighbour gets the same length?

answer.short:
$AC\approx10.8\text{ cm}$; AAS.

The two given angles and matching side determine congruent triangles.
answer.worked:
Draw $AB=12\text{ cm}$. At $A$, construct a perpendicular to $AB$ and bisect the right angle to obtain a $45^\circ$ ray. At $B$, construct a $60^\circ$ ray to $BA$ on the same side of $AB$, using an equilateral-triangle construction. Label the intersection of the rays $C$.

Measuring the constructed segment gives $AC\approx10.8\text{ cm}$ to the nearest millimetre.

Your neighbour's triangle has the same two angles and the matching side $AB$, so the triangles are congruent by AAS. Their matching sides $AC$ are therefore equal.

spec.description: Authored solution construction: a 12 cm base, a 45-degree ray at A, and a 60-degree ray at B intersect at C. Dashed auxiliary arcs illustrate angle constructions. Display size is schematic; students measure their own full-size construction.
spec.mathematics: A=(0,0), B=(12,0), C=(12sqrt(3)/(1+sqrt(3)),12sqrt(3)/(1+sqrt(3))). AC is approximately 10.8 cm.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Ajun claims to have constructed a triangle in which one side is $10\text{ cm}$ and the angles at each end of this side are $105^\circ$ and $80^\circ$. Comment on Ajun’s claim.

answer.worked:
$$105^\circ+80^\circ=185^\circ.$$

The two given angles already exceed the $180^\circ$ angle sum of a triangle. Ajun cannot have constructed such a triangle.

Page 9 establishes ruler-and-compasses construction as the local method.

Part b checks whether the two supplied angles can belong to a triangle. No trigonometric solution is introduced.

content.prompt: In each part below, say whether the two triangles are congruent. If they are congruent, write a congruence statement, including the appropriate congruence test.

spec.description: Horizontal pair of unshaded triangles with all six side measurements and vertex labels; no right-angle marks. Ordinary source blue lines become black.
spec.mathematics: AC=PR=10 cm; AB=PQ=20 cm; BC=QR=25 cm.
spec.answerVisibility: All supplied measurements remain visible; no congruence statement is supplied.

answer.worked: $AB=PQ=20\text{ cm}$, $BC=QR=25\text{ cm}$ and $AC=PR=10\text{ cm}$. The three matching sides are equal, so $\triangle ABC\equiv\triangle PQR$ (SSS).

spec.description: Horizontal pair, with the second triangle pointing down. Angle values remain inside their respective vertices.
spec.mathematics: BC=QP=3 m; angle B=angle P=70 degrees; angle C=angle Q=40 degrees.

answer.worked: $\angle B=\angle P=70^\circ$, $\angle C=\angle Q=40^\circ$ and the matching sides $BC=PQ=3\text{ m}$. Therefore $\triangle ABC\equiv\triangle RPQ$ (AAS).

spec.description: Horizontal pair of obtuse triangles with vertex I, not the numeral 1, on the first triangle.
spec.mathematics: Angle P=100 degrees; angle I=20 degrees; RI=12 cm. Angle C=60 degrees; angle T=100 degrees; UC=12 cm.
spec.answerVisibility: Missing angles and congruence result are not shown.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\angle R&=180^\circ-100^\circ-20^\circ\\\angle R&=60^\circ\\\angle U&=180^\circ-60^\circ-100^\circ\\\angle U&=20^\circ\end{align*}$$
Thus $\angle P=\angle T=100^\circ$, $\angle I=\angle U=20^\circ$ and $RI=CU=12\text{ cm}$. Therefore $\triangle RPI\equiv\triangle CTU$ (AAS).

spec.description: Horizontal pair of downward triangles. Side tick counts are three, two and four, preserving every marked correspondence.
spec.mathematics: TS=GF (three ticks), TP=GM (two ticks), SP=FM (four ticks).
spec.answerVisibility: Side marks only; no answer supplied.

answer.worked: The markings give $TS=GF$, $SP=FM$ and $TP=GM$. All three matching sides are equal, so $\triangle TSP\equiv\triangle GFM$ (SSS).

spec.description: Horizontal pair retaining the two 10 m labels on nonmatching sides and all four supplied angles.
spec.mathematics: EG=YR=10 m; angle G=angle Y=70 degrees; angle M=angle R=50 degrees.
spec.answerVisibility: No missing angle or result shown.

answer.worked: The remaining angles are $\angle E=\angle T=60^\circ$. Matching vertices are $E\leftrightarrow T$, $G\leftrightarrow Y$ and $M\leftrightarrow R$. The sides marked $10\text{ m}$ do not match: $EG$ is opposite $50^\circ$, whereas $YR$ is opposite $60^\circ$. Congruence would make $TY=YR=10\text{ m}$, requiring $\angle R=\angle T$, but $50^\circ\ne60^\circ$. Therefore the triangles are not congruent.

spec.description: Horizontal pair preserving double ticks on QF and AH, and all supplied angle labels.
spec.mathematics: QF=AH; angle Q=80 degrees; angle F=30 degrees; angle P=70 degrees; angle H=80 degrees.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\angle O&=180^\circ-80^\circ-30^\circ\\\angle O&=70^\circ\\\angle A&=180^\circ-70^\circ-80^\circ\\\angle A&=30^\circ\end{align*}$$
Thus $\angle O=\angle P=70^\circ$, $\angle F=\angle A=30^\circ$ and the marked matching sides $FQ=AH$. Therefore $\triangle OFQ\equiv\triangle PAH$ (AAS).

children.prompt: Use isosceles triangles to prove that $\angle APB=90^\circ$.

answer.short:
$\angle APB=90^\circ$.

Equal radii give two isosceles triangles, so $\angle APB=\alpha+\beta$; the angle sum of $\triangle APB$ gives $2\alpha+2\beta=180^\circ$.
answer.worked:
$OA=OP$ and $OB=OP$ because they are radii. Hence $\triangle AOP$ and $\triangle BOP$ are isosceles, so $\angle APO=\alpha$ and $\angle BPO=\beta$ (equal base angles).

Since $OP$ splits $\angle APB$, $\angle APB=\alpha+\beta$.

The angles of $\triangle APB$ sum to $180^\circ$:
$$\begin{align*}
2\alpha+2\beta&=180^\circ\\
\alpha+\beta&=90^\circ.
\end{align*}$$
Therefore $\angle APB=90^\circ$.

children.prompt: Let $H$ be the orthocentre of $\triangle ABC$. Prove that each of the four points $A$, $B$, $C$ and $H$ is the orthocentre of the triangle formed by the other three points. This is true in both cases – when $\triangle ABC$ is acute-angled and when $\triangle ABC$ is obtuse-angled.

answer.short:
$A$, $B$ and $C$ are the orthocentres of $\triangle BCH$, $\triangle ACH$ and $\triangle ABH$, respectively; $H$ is the orthocentre of $\triangle ABC$.

The same three perpendicular relationships supply the altitudes in each triangle, including when sides must be extended.
answer.worked:
Since $H$ is the orthocentre of $\triangle ABC$,
$$AH\perp BC,\qquad BH\perp AC,\qquad CH\perp AB.$$
In $\triangle BCH$, the line $BA$ is perpendicular to $CH$, the line $CA$ is perpendicular to $BH$, and the line $HA$ is perpendicular to $BC$. These three altitudes meet at $A$, so $A$ is its orthocentre.

In $\triangle ACH$, the line $AB$ is perpendicular to $CH$, the line $CB$ is perpendicular to $AH$, and the line $HB$ is perpendicular to $AC$. These three altitudes meet at $B$, so $B$ is its orthocentre.

In $\triangle ABH$, the line $AC$ is perpendicular to $BH$, the line $BC$ is perpendicular to $AH$, and the line $HC$ is perpendicular to $AB$. These three altitudes meet at $C$, so $C$ is its orthocentre.

Together with the given orthocentre $H$ of $\triangle ABC$, this proves all four statements. The argument uses perpendicular lines, so it applies to both acute-angled and obtuse-angled triangles, with sides extended where necessary.

entries.description:
Figures are copied everywhere – a photocopier can produce a copy of a figure, craft workers use copies of figures to create designs or patterns, copies of figures can be obtained by tracing, and so on.

The idea of a ‘copy’ also arises in geometry and is called ‘congruence’.

You have previously met the three kinds of geometrical transformation – translation, reflection and rotation. Two figures are called congruent if one is the image of the other when you apply one or more of these transformations.

We will see that two triangles are congruent when the sides and angles of one triangle are equal to the sides and angles of the other.

We can see from the examples above that when two triangles are congruent, paired sides have the same length and paired angles have the same size.
The rest of this chapter will develop four tests for two triangles to be congruent. At this stage, however, we simply note that:
If the vertices of two triangles can be paired up so that paired sides have the same length and paired angles have the same size, then they are congruent.
To demonstrate this, cut out one triangle and move it so that it lies exactly on top of the other triangle.
This process involves only translations and rotations, and a reflection if you have to turn the triangle over.

entries.description: When writing symbolic congruence statements, we use the symbol ≡ for ‘is congruent to’. For example, the triangles in the diagram on the previous page are congruent. This is written as: △ABC ≡ △DEF (Read this as ‘triangle ABC is congruent to triangle DEF.’) It is vitally important to write the vertices of the two triangles in matching order. In the statement above, we wrote the two triangles as △ABC and △DEF because the paired vertices are: A ↔ D and B ↔ E and A ↔ F. This attention to detail is useful when it comes to paired sides. We can read off the paired sides from the congruence statement △ABC ≡ △DEF in the natural way: AB ↔ DE and BC ↔ EF and CA ↔ FD.

The SSS congruence test

To prove that two triangles are congruent, it is not necessary to prove that they have three pairs of equal sides and three pairs of equal angles. In this section and the next, we will investigate the minimum amount of information needed to establish that two triangles are congruent.

Consider the three diagrams below.

entries.description:
We will construct a triangle with three given side lengths. Here is an example using the side lengths 12 cm, 10 cm and 5 cm.
Step 1: Draw an interval AB of length 12 cm.
Step 2: Draw a circle with centre A and radius 5 cm.
Step 3: Draw a circle with centre B and radius 10 cm crossing the first circle at C and C′.
Step 4: Join up the triangle ABC and the triangle ABC′.
The two triangles ABC and ABC′ are reflections of each other in AB and so are congruent.
Note: The three angles of any triangle are determined by the lengths of the three sides.

entries.description:
The four standard congruence tests for triangles
Two triangles are congruent if:
SSS: the three sides of one triangle are respectively equal to the three sides of the other triangle, or
AAS: two angles and one side of one triangle are respectively equal to two angles and the matching side of the other triangle, or
SAS: two sides and the included angle of one triangle are respectively equal to two sides and the included angle of the other triangle, or
RHS: the hypotenuse and one side of one right-angled triangle are respectively equal to the hypotenuse and one side of the other right-angled triangle.

Hence CA = CB (matching sides of congruent triangles)

entries.description:
Theorem: The interior angles of an equilateral triangle are all 60°.
Proof:
AC = AB (given)
so ∠C = ∠B (angles opposite equal sides)
Also CA = CB (given)
so ∠A = ∠B (angles opposite equal sides)
Therefore ∠A = ∠B = ∠C
Since the angles add to 180°, each angle must be 180 ÷ 3 = 60°.

entries.description: In this question, we prove that the base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal by proving that the triangle is congruent to itself. The proof is reputedly due to the Greek mathematician Pappus, who lived in Alexandria from about 290 CE to about 350 CE. Let △ABC be isosceles, with AC = BC.

entries.description:
Explain why the supposed ‘proof’ outlined below is invalid.
Let ABC be a triangle with ∠A = ∠B.
Mark the midpoint M of the base AB, and join CM.
Then △AMC ≡ △BMC.
Hence AC = BC.

entries.description:
The result ‘proven’ below is clearly false.
Explain why the reasoning is invalid.
Let △ABC be an isosceles triangle with AC = BC.
Let P be any point on the base AB, and join PC.
In the triangles ACP and BCP:
CP = CP (common)
CA = CB (given)
∠CAP = ∠CBP (base angles of isosceles △ABC)
so △ACP ≡ △BCP (SAS)
Hence AP = BP (matching sides of congruent triangles)
so P is the midpoint of AB.

‘If two sides and an obtuse non-included angle of one triangle are equal to two sides and a matching obtuse non-included angle of another triangle, then the triangles are congruent.’
Explain why this result is true.
